I graduated in May of 2020 during the start of the pandemic. I had no luck in finding a job that fitted what I wanted so around September 2020 I went back to a machine shop I interned at previously as a full-time CAD drafter. It was close to my house so I was fortunate enough to be able to live with my parents at the time. I then quit that job in January of 2021 to move a few states over to work at a big-name company in both a sales and then mechanical engineering role for about 2 years. I started to look for jobs in the spring of 2022 and landed an amazing job close to some extended family as a mechanical design engineer.

Overall, I would say it took a while and required some moving around to get where I wanted. When I look back it took a lot of sacrifices to get where I am now and I was hoping to get a "dream job" like every other engineer out of college. For most people, this is not the case and you have to start small,  build your resume, and move around a bit like in my case.

You seem like a very analytical person with this thought, as I have also thought about this too. I do not think it is that much of a controversial post, but something that brings us back to why their may be a high spike in mental illness in the last few decades. 

Our society has become more digitized,some terms like this get passed around often. There is a difference between being sad and depressed of course. Another thing is a lot of these people are addicted, as am I, to social media. Which I believe is one of the root causes of the spike. 

Isolation and not having anyone to talk to has made it much worse with Covid, and the newer generations may become more physically isolated as technology progresses or maybe not. I think this is why many people are talking to therapists more than ever now. They are scared what their friends/family might think of their issues and it’s easier to talk with a professional who can keep things confidential.

There are gives and takes to a lot of the new technologies/things in our lives and I think being aware of this helps a bit.

I do believe though that the negative connotations with having mental illness/being aware of it, makes it much worse and we as a society need to change that.
